newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU hopes for milestone summit with U.S. president.
newsitem.headline: EU hopes for milestone summit with U.S. president.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton and European Commission President Jacques Santer meet U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday for what has been billed in European circles as a "milestone" summit.
On the last lap of Ireland's six-month presidency of the European Union, Bruton will be looking to forge a new framework for EU-U.S. relations, an Irish government official said.
Trade with China and Beijing's future membership in the World Trade Organisation will also be addressed at the Washington meeting, one of two the EU and Washington hold each year.
But moves to establish more comprehensive ties between the EU and the United States could be hampered by continued European annoyance at U.S. anti-Cuban legislation enshrined in the Helms-Burton law.

"The European Union has adopted a very strong position against Helms-Burton," the Irish premier told a news conference on Saturday at the end of a two-day summit of EU leaders. "We will re-affirm EU opposition to this," he added.

Under the terms of the legislation, which was introduced earlier this year and is designed to bring democracy to Cuba, firms doing certain types of business with the Caribbean island risk punitive action in the United States..

Emphasing Europe's different approach to Cuba, the EU said at the weekend it would consider negotiating a trade accord with Havana, while at the same time saying the respect of human rights and moves to political reform were a condition.

In a communique following an EU summit in Dublin, the leaders also scolded Washington, saying it should pursue means against Cuba "other than unilateral action at the expense of closer partners with shared values."
The Commission's Santer sought to play down the dispute.
"Our summit with Clinton won't just be about Helms-Burton," he told a news conference. "We have much more in common with the U.S. than what divides us," he added.

The December 16 meeting marks the first anniversary of the EU's adoption of a new formal approach to its relations with the United States. In the final document to the Dublin summit on Saturday, the 15-nation bloc said it expected the meeting with Clinton would mark "another milestone" in EU-U.S. relations.

An Irish official said that the EU and U.S. had previously concentrated much of their efforts on joint security concerns. "Now we need a more all-embracing relationship to reflect the end of the cold war," he said.
"We have to develop common interests on scientific issues, development aid and trade matters," he added.

On the trade front, EU foreign ministers agreed last week that China's role in the WTO should be on the agenda at Monday's summit. China has indicated in recent meetings that it wants to renew its membership drive for the world trade body.
The EU wants to gauge America's attitude and perhaps adopt a common approach to Beijing.
